findings.resolution_hint: For each listed docstring, drop the `§N[.M]` reference from the rendered text (state the invariant itself, as the surrounding sentence already does) and, if the citation is still wanted for a maintainer, move it to the `#` comment immediately above the function/module, mirroring the file's own top-of-file `# ... (ARCHITECTURE §N)` comment.
findings.description: RULE.DOC.NO_DEAD_REFS states verbatim: "A rendered docstring or a thrown error message cites no section number, repo path or inaccessible source, and reads complete at the REPL where links are dead. ... Section citations and design rationale stay in `#` comments and the rationale documents." This is enforced by SCAN.DEAD_REF's `§\s?[0-9]` pattern, applied only to text `prose_lines` extracts as docstring content (a triple-quoted string whose opening `"""` sits alone on its line — the house form both `Reflection.docstrings` and the scan engine key on, which is why a header comment or a `const X = """..."""` data string is correctly exempt). At least 10 real, rendered docstrings across the src surface embed an ARCHITECTURE.md section number (§6.1, §6.2, §6.3, §5, §7.3, §8, §12, §12.B) directly in their prose — not in a `#` comment above the function, where the rule says such a citation belongs (and where the identical fact is often already stated, in the very same file's top-of-file comment). A reader at the REPL (`?GBGCodingTools.gate`, `?TestHarness.selftest`, `?Doctor`, etc.) or on the built API page sees a bare section number with no way to resolve it — exactly the failure this rule exists to prevent. This is a class, not one instance.
findings.title: Docstrings across src cite ARCHITECTURE.md section numbers, which RULE.DOC.NO_DEAD_REFS forbids

locations: src/TestHarness.jl:301-302 — "so `Config.read`, `Git.run` and `Scan.report` denote the package's function and not the `Base` export they collide with"
findings.resolution_hint: Replace `Scan.report` with a real third example of a package-owned name shadowing a Base export (or drop it, keeping `Config.read`/`Git.run`), and re-check any other inline prose example in this docstring resolves to an actual qualified name.
findings.description: The docstring of `TestHarness.resolve_function` offers `Config.read`, `Git.run` and `Scan.report` as worked examples of a package module owning a name that also collides with a `Base` export. `Config.read` and `Git.run` are genuine (module `Config` in src/CLI/Config.jl owns `read`, extending `Base.read`; module `Git` in src/CLI/Git.jl owns `run`, extending `Base.run`), but no module named `Scan` exists anywhere in the codebase (`grep -rn 'module Scan\b' src/` returns nothing): `report` is a plain function defined directly inside `module GBGCodingTools` by src/Scan.jl (`function report(results::AbstractVector{ScanResult}; io::IO = stdout)`, line 455), included without its own `module Scan ... end` wrapper. Its real qualified name is `GBGCodingTools.report`, never `Scan.report`. The example also fails on its own terms even corrected: `Base` exports no `report` for `GBGCodingTools.report` to collide with, unlike `read`/`run`, so it demonstrates nothing about the ownership-vs-Base-collision point the sentence makes.
findings.title: `resolve_function` docstring cites a nonexistent `Scan.report` qualified name

findings.title: "refuses only because a round... is open" is not what the code actually checks
findings.description: `docs_build_skipped` (src/DocLints.jl:44) treats any `code == 1` together with a nonempty `frozen_rounds(cfg, "check-docs", "check-consistency")` as skippable; it never checks that an open docs-instrument round is the sole source of the refusal. `gate()` (src/CLI/Gate.jl:26) can return 1 for an unrelated reason that is independently true at the same time — e.g. an open round of a disabled instrument, added regardless of `wanted` and regardless of `CI` — while a check-docs/check-consistency round also happens to be open. In that concurrent case `gate_or_skip` prints the benign SKIPPED message and returns `true`, silently absorbing the unrelated disabled-instrument refusal into what reads as a routine, expected skip.

findings.description: RULE.TEST.RULE_WITH_CHECK defines `weakness` as "a check is possible and none is built." For RULE.CIT.DOI ("Every reference carries a clickable DOI... identical in every copy") a check IS built: SCAN.DOI_CROSSCHECK's own header comment names RULE.CIT.DOI as one of the two rules it enforces, and its `require_doi` block (live in this package, tier hard, config flag true) is exactly that enforcement. RULES.toml nonetheless records RULE.CIT.DOI as an unpaid-check weakness — the rulebook misreporting its own coverage, the one thing RULE.TEST.RULE_WITH_CHECK exists to keep honest. findings.description: docs-rubric.md's only rule governing how a docstring's arguments are documented, RULE.DOC.ARGS_FORM, mandates the prose lead-in `The arguments are:` and never a `# Arguments` Markdown heading; this package's own docstrings confirm it (0 uses of a `# Arguments` heading vs 30 uses of `The arguments are:`). Yet RULE.DOC.SHAPE's ordering clause, and the scan enforcing it, test specifically for a `# Arguments` heading — a structural element no other rule in this file ever sanctions the corpus to produce. (docs/ARCHITECTURE.md shows this heading is a different fleet consumer's (IT's) argument-doc style, so the clause is a deliberate cross-consumer accommodation, but that provenance is not disclosed anywhere in the rendered docs-rubric.md itself.) Failure scenario: a reader of docs-rubric.md in isolation — exactly how it is meant to be read, rendered whole into every consumer's session — hits this clause with no antecedent, and either concludes the rulebook is self-contradictory (ARGS_FORM bans the heading it implies) or hunts for a heading form that, for this package, never legitimately exists.

locations: templates/commit-message.tmpl:5-6 — "The instruments this package carried in `.claude/commands/` are replaced by the tool's, at the pinned version above."
src/CLI/Init.jl:517-518 — only reads `.claude/commands/check-consistency/seed_defects.py`, never deletes/moves the directory
src/CLI/Doctor.jl:437-444 — `LEG.COMMANDS` FAILs while `.claude/commands/{check-docs,check-consistency,bug-hunt,audit-changes}*` files are still present
findings.resolution_hint: Either have `gbg init --migrate` actually remove the stale `.claude/commands/<instrument>*` files before this message is written, or soften the sentence, e.g. 'The instruments this package carried in `.claude/commands/` are superseded by the tool's `.claude/skills/` stubs above; remove the old `.claude/commands/` files in this commit (`gbg doctor`'s `LEG.COMMANDS` checks for them).'
findings.description: This template is rendered by `gbg init --migrate` into `.gbg/scratch/commit-message.txt` and is meant to be committed verbatim. It states as accomplished fact that the old `.claude/commands/` instruments were 'replaced', but no code under src/ or ext/ deletes, moves, or overwrites anything under `.claude/commands/` — `migrate_seeds` only reads `check-consistency/seed_defects.py` from it. The doctor carries a dedicated check, `LEG.COMMANDS`, whose job is to FAIL when those legacy files are still present after migration, i.e. the tool's own design treats 'still there' as the default post-migration state a human must fix, not something `gbg init --migrate`/`gbg sync` accomplishes. A session committing this message verbatim without separately deleting `.claude/commands/` records a false claim in permanent git history.
findings.title: commit-message.tmpl asserts a `.claude/commands/` replacement the tool never performs

findings.description: README.md's 'Managed headers' paragraph describes exactly two header shapes, both single-line, naming the template and version. In practice `claude-md.block` and `gitignore.block` — both class G in the table above this paragraph — use a third, undocumented shape: a `begin ... end` bracket pair (with an inline `sha256:{{sha256}}` stamp for CLAUDE.md) produced by a different code path (`Sync.managed_block`/`BLOCKS`, Sync.jl:227-256) than the `managed_header` function the paragraph's `#`-commented example matches verbatim. That `:hash` branch of `managed_header` is dead code — only `managed_header(:html, ...)` is ever invoked, and only for the `.gbg/policy/*.md` copies. A reader relying on README.md's stated contract to understand how a hand-edit of `.gitignore`'s or `CLAUDE.md`'s managed block is detected is misled about the actual mechanism.
findings.title: README.md's 'Managed headers' section omits the begin/end block convention it should describe

locations: src/CLI/Rounds.jl:333-339 (docstring)
src/CLI/Rounds.jl:345 (sha-changed → :rejected, before parsing)
src/CLI/Rounds.jl:346-358 (unparsable/schema/lane/verdict DEAD branches, each with mv(...))
src/CLI/Rounds.jl:360 (zero-findings-and-empty-checked DEAD branch, no mv(...))
findings.resolution_hint: Either add the missing mv(...) quarantine to the zero-findings/empty-checked DEAD branch (matching the docstring), or reword the docstring to state that only the schema/parse/lane/verdict DEAD reasons quarantine the file while the empty-corpus DEAD reason does not; and reorder either the code (check DEAD content reasons before the sha-changed check) or the docstring (state explicitly that a changed sha is checked, and reported, before the file's content is even read).
findings.description: classify_lane's docstring reads: 'The status is `:dead` — absent; renamed to `<name>.rejected.json` beside itself when unparsable, when it fails the instrument's schema, or when it is schema-valid but its own `lane` field names a different lane... or when its own `verdict` contradicts its findings...; or well-formed with zero findings AND an empty `checked[]`... Then `:rejected` (present but its sha changed since first sight), `:empty`..., `:truncated`..., or `:live`.' Read naturally, every DEAD reason (including the last, zero-findings-and-empty-checked) gets the file renamed to `.rejected.json`, and REJECTED is determined only after the DEAD checks have had their turn. The body does the opposite on both counts: line 345, `first_sha !== nothing && first_sha != sha && return (:rejected, nothing, sha, "changed since first sight")`, fires before the file is even parsed — so a lane file that both changed sha since first sight AND is unparsable/schema-invalid/mislabelled is reported REJECTED, never DEAD, and is never quarantined by the mv() the other DEAD branches use. Separately, the docstring's own last-listed DEAD reason — 'well-formed with zero findings AND an empty `checked[]`' — maps to line 360, `(n == 0 && isempty(get(data, "checked", []))) && return (:dead, data, sha, "zero findings AND empty checked[] — a dead lane, not a clean one")` — which, unlike every other DEAD branch above it (lines 348, 353, 356, 358), calls no `mv(...)` at all: the file is left at its original path, not renamed to `.rejected.json`. So a lane that reports zero findings with an empty `checked[]` is graded DEAD (correctly) but is never quarantined, contradicting the docstring's 'renamed to `<name>.rejected.json` beside itself when ... or well-formed with zero findings AND an empty `checked[]`.'
findings.title: classify_lane checks REJECTED (sha-changed) before any DEAD content check, and the last DEAD branch never quarantines the file — both contradicting the docstring's ordering and blanket rename claim

locations: src/Scan.jl:36-37 (ScanResult.population docstring)
src/Scan.jl:449-451 (report() docstring)
src/Scan.jl:457 (dead(r) = r.population == 0 && r.exempted == 0)
findings.resolution_hint: Either drop the `&& r.exempted == 0` conjunct from dead(r) so a zero-population scan is always DEAD regardless of ledger exemptions (matching the docstrings), or amend both docstrings to state the real rule: 'population zero AND no ledger exemption is DEAD; a zero-population scan the ledger has exempted is reported ok instead.'
findings.description: ScanResult's docstring states unconditionally: 'population — ...; zero means the scan measured nothing and is DEAD.' report()'s own docstring reinforces this as an invariant: 'A scan whose population is zero measured nothing and is DEAD whatever else it did — that refusal is the point of the counter,' and further: 'Its hits are still printed: a scan that measured nothing yet hit something is a scan whose own counter is wrong, and dropping the evidence hides which one.' The actual predicate is `dead(r) = r.population == 0 && r.exempted == 0` (line 457) — an extra `exempted == 0` conjunct the docstrings never mention. When a scan measures zero population yet its raw hits (before the ledger) are non-empty and the ledger then exempts/disables the scan (`apply_ledger` sets `exempted = length(hits)`), `dead(r)` is false: the result is routed into the plain 'ok' branch of report(), never into the DEAD branch that prints the offending hits. That is precisely the scenario the docstring says cannot happen ('DEAD whatever else it did', 'dropping the evidence hides which one') — the code drops exactly that evidence when the scan is also ledger-exempted.
findings.title: report()'s DEAD predicate requires exempted == 0, silently contradicting the docstrings' claim that a zero-population scan is DEAD 'whatever else it did'

findings.description: resolve_hats' docstring says a hat 'carries `key`; the persona with its placeholders filled; and the four fields below' — then names exactly four: substrate, needs, anchor, not_applicable. The dict actually pushed at line 306-307 carries a fifth data field beyond key and persona: `"role" => get(h, "role", "")`. The claim of an exact count ('the four fields below') is therefore off by one against the body. Compounding it operationally: `role` is never read anywhere the roster is consumed afterward — `roster_record` (line 399) and `render_args`' `a["hats"]` projection (line 538) both list out only key/persona_path/substrate/needs/anchor(/not_applicable), never role — so the field the docstring omits is also a value nothing downstream ever uses.
findings.title: resolve_hats' docstring enumerates 'the four fields below' but the returned hat dict carries a fifth, undocumented field ('role') that is also never propagated onward

locations: src/CLI/Rounds.jl:816-817 (abandon docstring)
src/CLI/Rounds.jl:837-838 (open_ids computed from findings.json)
findings.resolution_hint: Reword the parenthetical to 'all non-seeded banked ids when no pass was graded' (a seeded finding is never a real defect and is correctly excluded per RULE.INST.SEEDS; the docstring just needs to say so).
findings.description: abandon's docstring: 'It writes `abandoned = {reason, open_ids}` with every id still open (all banked ids when no pass was graded)...'. The body, for the no-graded-pass branch, is `open_ids = [f["id"] for f in JSON3.read(...)["findings"] if !get(f, "seeded", false)]` — this explicitly drops every finding with `seeded == true`, so the recorded open_ids is NOT 'all banked ids' but 'all non-seeded banked ids.' A round banked with seeded findings and abandoned before any pass is graded would have its abandoned.open_ids silently omit the seeded ones, contrary to the docstring's literal claim.
findings.title: abandon's docstring says open_ids becomes 'all banked ids' when no pass was graded, but the body excludes seeded findings

findings.title: "act verifier" / "state verifier" and the HONORED/LINE-ONLY verdict vocabulary are used with no definition anywhere in the source
findings.description: A cold reader meets `?GBGCodingTools.demote` (Demote.jl is included right after Doctor.jl, well before Passes.jl) and is immediately handed four unglossed terms of art at once: "act verdict", "the act verifier" (vs. "the state verifier", elsewhere called "the blind verifier" — three names for what turn out to be two roles), "class_surfaces", and "swept". None is a plain-English read: an "act verifier" does not mean a verifier that acts, and "swept" here means specifically "a location a finding names that the fix pass's diff touched" (RULE.DOC.CLASS_SWEEP's sense), not the ordinary sense used two lines earlier in Reflection.jl ("whose `src` surface names the files swept", meaning merely "read"). The closed verdict vocabulary itself — `HONORED`, `LINE-ONLY`, and later `PHANTOM`/`UNFIXED`/`ABSENT`/`NOT-A-DEFECT` (Witnesses.jl, Passes.jl) — is never enumerated or explained as a vocabulary anywhere a `?name` lookup would land; each docstring just uses the members as already-known constants. I verified this is not merely a link I missed: I grepped the whole `src/` and `ext/` tree for "act verifier", "state verifier", "blind verifier", "class_surfaces", "HONORED", "LINE-ONLY" and every occurrence is inside a docstring or comment that USES the term, none DEFINES it (the closest thing to a definition, RULE.INST.SELF_REPORT's "the act verifier sees the diff, the state verifier is blind", lives only in the policy rulebook, which a `?name` REPL read never surfaces). By contrast, every other overloaded-but-central term in this package (`consumer`, `instrument`, `round`, `lane`, `hat`, `gate`, the three senses of `anchor`, `surface`, `managed file`, DEAD/REJECTED/EMPTY/TRUNCATED lane statuses) gets exactly this kind of module-docstring or first-use definition elsewhere in the same corpus, which is what makes its absence here conspicuous rather than a house style.

findings.title: severity-recheck.js and attack-design.js write A.round without validating it was supplied
findings.description: Both scripts document 'round' as part of Args and write it into their output, but neither's required-arg guard (`for (const k of [...]) if (A[k]===undefined) throw`) includes 'round', unlike every sibling script that writes round (lanes.js, panel.js, audit.js, hunt.js, dismissals.js all validate it).
